world_behind.title: The second reading: Isaiah 49
world_behind.text: Where chapter 20 scolded and promised, this text turns to the Servant: called from the womb, hidden like a weapon, despairing of his labor, and given as "a light to the Gentiles" (v. 6). The reading also carries the fullest scattering-and-gathering promises Nephi has, which is what his interpretation in chapter 22 will spend itself on.

world_behind.title: The Servant's double identity
world_behind.text: The figure is addressed as "my servant, O Israel" (v. 3) yet labors to "bring Jacob again to him" (v. 5): Israel personified, and a person sent to Israel, in the same poem. The ambiguity is ancient and productive; the record will read the Servant both ways, nation and Messiah, without forcing a choice.

world_behind.title: A weapons cache of words
world_behind.text: "a sharp sword" (v. 2), "a polished shaft" (v. 2), hidden in hand and quiver: the Servant is armament kept concealed until needed. Polishing a shaft is fletcher's work, slow abrasion toward flight; the figure gives the delay itself a purpose, which a family twenty years into a detour could hear.

world_behind.title: Engraved palms
world_behind.text: "I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands" (v. 16) answers Zion's complaint with the era's most permanent writing technology, the same verb this record uses for its own plates. A name written on skin wears off; one graven cannot. The verse puts Zion where a workman cannot look without seeing her.

spans.text: I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands

world_behind.title: Nursing kings
world_behind.text: "kings shall be thy nursing fathers" (v. 23) inverts the ancient order: monarchs who took tribute and children now carry the children home and feed them. Court prostration ("lick up the dust of thy feet" (v. 23)) is aimed at Zion, not from her: the exiles' humiliations run backward.

spans.text: kings shall be thy nursing fathers

world_behind.title: Sinim and the compass points
world_behind.text: The gathered come from north, west, and "the land of Sinim" (v. 12), a place-name so far its location was already obscure: the point is horizon-breaking distance. For hearers who themselves came by sea to a land off every map, the roll call of far places includes, implicitly, theirs.

words.text: "made me a polished shaft" (v. 2): an arrow worked smooth so it flies true, then hidden "in his quiver" (v. 2). The verb costs time and friction, and the hiddenness is storage, not neglect. The Servant's obscurity, and every believer's, is here a weapon's waiting.

"shall the prey be taken from the mighty" (v. 24): the word admits what Israel is at the question's asking, something caught and being consumed. The next verse answers with the chapter's boldest mechanics: the Lord contends with the contender, and the meal is taken back out of the predator's mouth.

phrases.term: all ye that are broken off
phrases.text: The block's largest variant: before the KJV's opening ("Listen, O isles, unto me," Isa. 49:1), the record carries a full verse addressing "all ye that are broken off and are driven out" (v. 1), scattered "because of the wickedness of the pastors of my people" (v. 1). The added preface aims the whole poem at exactly the audience Nephi named at 19:24, a broken-off branch, before the first KJV word arrives.

spans.text: all ye that are broken off and are driven out

cites.quote: because of the wickedness of the pastors of my people

spans.text: because of the wickedness of the pastors of my people

phrases.text: Where the KJV reads only "and in a day of salvation have I helped thee" (Isa. 49:8), the record inserts the address "O isles of the sea" (v. 8), and later "my servant" (v. 8) for the covenant-giving. The isles, Zenos's word for the scattered (19:16), are written into the poem's second-person: the far branches are not eavesdropping on Israel's mail; they are named in it.

phrases.term: the feet of those who are in the east shall be established
phrases.text: The KJV's burst of praise ("Sing, O heavens; and be joyful, O earth; and break forth into singing, O mountains," Isa. 49:13) gains two clauses: "the feet of those who are in the east shall be established" (v. 13) and "for they shall be smitten no more" (v. 13). The variant adds standing ground and an end of striking to the singing: comfort with substance in it for people mid-scattering.

phrases.term: but he will show that he hath not
phrases.text: Zion's complaint ("The Lord hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me" (v. 14)) ends the verse in the KJV (Isa. 49:14); the record adds the narrator's assurance: "but he will show that he hath not" (v. 14). The variant refuses to let the accusation stand even one verse: the demonstration (sucking child, graven palms) is announced before it begins.

phrases.term: I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands
phrases.text: The answer to forgottenness is engraving, this record's own verb for permanence: what is cut into metal, or flesh, outlasts every lapse of attention. Zion is not remembered the way a task is remembered but the way a scar is carried, and the walls of the ruined city stand "continually before me" (v. 16).

phrases.term: I will lift up mine hand to the Gentiles
phrases.text: The gathering's mechanism: a signal ("my standard to the people" (v. 22)), then foreign arms carrying "thy sons" (v. 22) and "thy daughters" (v. 22) home. Jacob will requote this passage almost immediately (2 Ne. 6:6) and Nephi will interpret it in the next chapter: of everything in the reading, this is the verse the small plates cannot leave alone.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: Called, hidden, named
verses.text: The expanded address gathers the broken-off, then the Servant speaks: called "from the womb" (v. 1), mouth a sword, body an arrow, hidden in hand and quiver, and told "Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified" (v. 3). Election in this poem is armament and concealment both; being unseen is part of the commission.

cites.quote: Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified

spans.text: Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified

verses.label: v. 4–6
verses.title: The Servant's discouragement, and the raise
verses.text: The astonishing admission: "I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for naught" (v. 4). The answer is not consolation but enlargement: "It is a light thing" (v. 6) to restore Jacob only; the Servant gets the Gentiles and "the ends of the earth" (v. 6) added to his brief. Heaven's cure for a called man's despair is more calling.

cites.quote: I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for naught

spans.text: I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for naught

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: Despised, then attended by kings
verses.text: To "him whom man despiseth" (v. 7): kings shall arise, princes worship, "because of the Lord that is faithful" (v. 7). The Servant is made "a covenant of the people" (v. 8) in person, and his first commands are jailbreak: "to the prisoners: Go forth" (v. 9); to the darkened, show yourselves. The reversal runs on God's faithfulness, not the Servant's reception.

cites.quote: because of the Lord that is faithful

spans.text: because of the Lord that is faithful

verses.label: v. 10–13
verses.title: The shepherded return
verses.text: No hunger, no smiting heat, springs of water, mountains made "a way" (v. 11): the exodus mercies reissued for a worldwide return from north, west, and Sinim. The added clauses of verse 13 plant feet and end the smiting, and heaven and earth are ordered to sing over it.

verses.label: v. 14–16
verses.title: The complaint and the engraving
verses.text: Zion speaks for every exile: forsaken, forgotten. The reply stacks three permanences: a nursing mother's body ("can a woman forget her sucking child" (v. 15)), the concession that even she might ("Yea, they may forget" (v. 15)), and then the palms, graven, where forgetting has no mechanism. The record's God does not promise to remember; he shows the inscription.

cites.quote: can a woman forget her sucking child

spans.text: can a woman forget her sucking child

verses.label: v. 17–21
verses.title: The crowded desolation
verses.text: Children hurry back, the waste places grow "too narrow" (v. 19), and the bereaved mother hears children she cannot account for: "Who hath begotten me these" (v. 21) and "Behold, I was left alone" (v. 21). The gathering outruns Zion's own arithmetic; she is dressed in her returned children "as a bride" (v. 18) while still asking where they came from.

verses.label: v. 22–26
verses.title: The hand, the kings, the rescue
verses.text: The standard goes up, Gentile arms carry the children, kings turn nurse, and the lawyer's question ("shall the prey be taken from the mighty" (v. 24)) gets its answer: "even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away" (v. 25), for "I will contend with him that contendeth with thee" (v. 25). The reading ends with all flesh knowing the Redeemer, and Nephi's brothers, on cue, will ask what it means.

chapter.title: The text answers its introduction
chapter.text: Nephi promised hope for "all ye that are broken off" (v. 1) at 19:24, and this block's opening variant addresses precisely that congregation before Isaiah's first word. Reading and audience interlock so tightly that the likening method looks less like application than like delivery of addressed mail.

cites.quote: all ye that are broken off

spans.text: all ye that are broken off

chapter.title: A Servant for the despairing servant
chapter.text: The poem's center is a called man who thinks he has failed and is answered with a larger commission. Nephi, whose workings in the spirit weary his joints (19:20) and whose own mission to his brothers keeps failing, reads aloud a text in which vain labor is a stage of the call, not its refutation.

chapter.title: The variants aim the poem outward
chapter.text: Each major divergence (the broken-off preface, the isles-of-the-sea address, the established feet in the east, the he-will-show assurance) widens the audience or firms the promise. As in chapter 20, the brass-plates text is the more explicit reading, and its explicitness runs toward the scattered.

chapter.title: Forgottenness is met with anatomy
chapter.text: The chapter's argument against divine forgetting is physical: womb, breast, engraved palms, a body that cannot lose Zion. For hearers whose deepest fear is being a forgotten branch, the reading relocates their names from God's memory to God's flesh.

chapter.title: The gathering has logistics
chapter.text: Standard, signal, carrying arms, nursing kings, contested prey: this is not vague hope but mechanism, and it is why chapter 22 exists. Nephi's brothers ask their first real doctrinal question because this chapter's promises are concrete enough to argue about.

chapter.title: Reversal is the poem's grammar
chapter.text: Despised to worshiped, prisoner to fed flock, bereaved to overcrowded, prey to rescued, oppressor to self-devoured: every station of exile is run backward. The record reads history the same way, which is why its editors keep this chapter close for the rest of the volume.

chapter.title: The unit's hinge to interpretation
chapter.text: Two chapters of assigned reading end with the strongest possible claims about the isles and the Gentiles, and no application sentence. Chapter 22 opens with the brothers asking whether all this is spiritual or temporal: the reading has done its work, and the discussion can begin.

applications.title: Read your obscurity as a quiver
applications.text: If your gifts feel hidden, ask whether they are being stored rather than shelved: polished, protected, and dated for a flight not yet called. Keep sharpening in the dark; concealment in this poem is custody.

applications.title: Answer despair with assignment
applications.text: When labor feels spent for naught, notice the poem's therapy: the Servant's cure was a bigger errand, not a rest. Take on the small next assignment (a person, a class, a calling) and let enlargement do what consolation cannot.

applications.title: Keep a graven list
applications.text: Write the names you are tempted to believe God has forgotten, your own included, and read them against the palms verse. Then practice the divine method on your own scale: put the people you must not forget where your work forces you to see them.

applications.title: Audit your complaint
applications.text: Zion's "the Lord hath forsaken me" was answerable, and the record's variant says so immediately. State your own version of the complaint out loud, then list the demonstrations already on record. Most forsakenness dissolves under inventory.

applications.title: Carry someone's children
applications.text: In the gathering, outsiders do the carrying. Find one practical way this season to be the Gentile arms of the promise: transport, meals, tuition, testimony, whatever brings someone's sons and daughters nearer home.

applications.title: Wait without shame
applications.text: The verse's last clause is the whole program: "they shall not be ashamed that wait for me" (v. 23). Name the promise you are tired of waiting on, and retire the embarrassment of still believing it; in this chapter the waiters are the ones vindicated.

questions.text: What has the delay in my life polished that immediate use would have left rough?
When I last said "I have labored in vain," what did I do with the feeling, and what does the Servant's example suggest?
Whose forgetting do I actually fear, God's or people's, and does my prayer life know the difference?
What would change today if I believed my name were engraved where God cannot avoid seeing it?
Where has God's arithmetic already outrun mine: what do I have that I never begot and cannot account for?
Which "mighty" currently holds something of mine, and do I believe the contend-with-the-contender clause applies to it?
